records.text: Fork in play. One piece hits several targets in the same move, and a single answer might not save them all. Spot the attacker, then count its targets.
Fork spotted, and it's theirs. After this, one of their pieces can reach several targets in one go. Scan where their pieces can land before committing to a move.
Fork left on the table. A different move would have hit several targets with one piece. Find that move and lock the pattern in.
Pin locked. A piece is held to its king now, and stepping off the line would expose that king. Mark the pinned piece and watch what it can no longer do.
Pin incoming. This move lets the other side tie a piece to its own king, so it can't leave the line without exposing that king. Check every line to the king before moving.
Pin missed. Another move could have frozen a piece in front of its king. Go back, find the line, and mark the piece that would have been stuck.
Skewer on the line. The front piece takes the hit, and once it steps aside, the piece behind it is open. Read the line front to back.
Skewer alert. Two pieces share a line, and this move lets the other side aim down it. If the front piece moves, the one behind can be hit. Watch shared lines.
Skewer missed. A different move lined up an attack through a front piece to the one behind it. Find that line and run the idea again.
Defender down. This move captures a piece that was guarding something, and that something may now be loose. Spot what it was covering.
Defender exposed. This move lets the other side capture a key defender, and whatever it guarded could lose its cover. Know which defenders matter before every move.
Defender left standing. Another move could have taken it off the board and left its charge exposed. Hunt the defender first next time.
Back-rank pattern. The enemy king sits behind its own pieces with nowhere to step, and this move goes straight at that weakness. Check the escape squares and confirm they're shut.
Back-rank pattern. The king is boxed in by its own pieces, and this move opens a route to a back-rank mate for the other side. Make an escape square before it's needed.
Back-rank chance missed. The enemy king was hemmed in by its own pieces, and a back-rank mate idea was there. Scan the back rank whenever a king has no exit.
Promotion run. This move is about getting a pawn to the last rank, where it turns into a new piece. Count the squares left and spot what can stop it.
Runner alert. This gives one of their pawns a real shot at promotion. Count its squares to the last rank and find the blocker.
Promotion route missed. A stronger move pushed a pawn toward the last rank, and this one doesn't. When a pawn is that close, count first.
Discovered attack. One piece steps aside and the piece behind it opens fire along the line. Watch the line that opens, not just the piece that moved.
Discovery threat. This move lets the other side shift a front piece and unmask an attack from the one behind it. Scan their stacked pieces before moving.
Discovery missed. Another move could have stepped a piece aside to let the one behind it attack. Find the stacked pair and run it again.
Double attack. Two threats from one move, and one reply often can't cover both. Name both threats, fast.
Two threats incoming. This move hands the other side a double attack, and one answer may not handle both. Before moving, check their most forcing reply.
Double attack missed. Two threats were sitting in a stronger move. Forcing two-threat moves come first in the scan.
Deflection. A defender gets pulled off its post, and the thing it was covering opens up. Spot the defender's job, then the move that broke it.
Deflection threat. After this move, the other side can drag a defender off duty. Map every defender's job.
Deflection missed. Another move could have pulled a defender off its job and opened what it guarded. Find the overworked defender next time.
Loose piece, collected. Nothing was guarding it, so it comes off for free. First scan, every move: loose pieces.
Loose piece missed. A free piece was there for another move to grab. Free material comes first, every time.
Hanging piece. This move leaves a piece with no guard, and the other side can take it. Every move, run the guard check on every piece.
Guard pulled. This move takes away a piece's only real defender, and now the other side can capture what it was covering. Know a defender's job before it leaves its post.
Threat ignored. The opponent's last move attacked a piece, and this move doesn't answer it, so that piece can be captured. After every opponent move, ask what it now attacks.
Bad trade. This capture runs into a recapture that takes a more valuable piece. Count the full exchange, every capture, before starting it.
Piece in play. A minor piece is off its starting post and in the fight. Mark its new post and what it now reaches.
Development available. A minor piece could have entered play with a different move. Weigh it against the move played.
Open file claimed by the rook. No pawns of either color block the file. Note the squares the rook now controls.
Open file available. A different move would have given a rook a file clear of pawns from both sides. Rooks belong on files like that.
Semi-open file. The rook has no pawns of its own in front, only an enemy pawn somewhere along the file. That enemy pawn is the thing to watch.
Rook upgrade available. A different move would have put a rook where it has no pawns of its own ahead, only an enemy pawn. Compare the two placements.
Passed pawn. No enemy pawn stands ahead of it on its file or the two beside it, so only pieces can stop it. Mark it and track its route.
Passer available. Another move would have created a pawn with no enemy pawns ahead on its file or the neighboring ones. Note the difference.
Passer advancing. The pawn was already passed, and now it's one step closer to the last rank. Count what's left.
Push available. The passed pawn could have marched with another move. Measure the distance it would have gained.
Isolated pawn. No friendly pawn sits on either neighboring file, so pawns can't defend it. Mark it as a structural target.
Isolation in the alternative. A different move would have left a pawn with no friendly pawn on the files next to it. Weigh that against what was played.
Cover added. Guard assigned to a piece that had none. Check the connection and keep it.
Cover available. A different move would have put a guard next to a lone piece. Compare which pieces stay guarded each way.
Unguarded piece. One piece is now standing guardless. That isn't a loss yet; test whether anything can actually reach it.
Unguarded in the alternative. A different move would have stripped a piece of its guard. Undefended doesn't mean lost, so check what could reach it.
Escape square open. The king now has a legal square it couldn't use before. Pinpoint the piece that cleared the path.
Escape square available. Another move would have handed the king a fresh legal square. Identify the piece that had to shift.
Castled. King and rook both moved in one turn, the rook landing next to the king. Check both new squares.
Castling available. The alternative was to castle, shifting king and rook together. Compare the king's safety each way.
Bishop pair broken. This capture leaves one side without bishops on both square colors. Note which color is now uncovered.
Bishop pair target. A different move would have taken a bishop and split the other side's pair. Weigh that trade.
Doubled pawns. Two pawns of one color now share a file, and they can't protect each other. Log the structure change.
Doubled pawns in the alternative. A different move would have stacked two same-color pawns on one file. Weigh that cost.
Mate allowed. Forced checkmate for the other side, straight from this move. Run the attack back one forcing move at a time and find where the defense broke.
Mate missed. The board had a forced checkmate, and the game move skipped it. Rule one: check every check first.
Sacrifice holds. Even when the material is taken, the idea survives in the searched line. Play the capture and follow what comes next.
Only move, found. Of everything searched, this alone kept the position playable; the rest lost. Lock that defense in.
Precision required. Of the searched moves, the edge survived with this one alone, and the rest were losing. Remember the resource.
Incoming capture. Right after this move, the other side has something to take. Clear that threat first.
Check incoming. The strongest reply comes with check, so the king is the first thing to deal with.
Better move available. The engine has its own pick here. Set both moves up and race the replies.
Value dropped. The engine rates its best move above this one. Compare the replies to find where the difference shows up.
Strong move. It holds up against everything the engine examined. Lock in why it works.
Solid. Most of the position's value survives, even though the engine's top pick is different. Compare the two for the last bit of value.
Natural, and wrong. The human-move model reads this as a likely choice, but the engine finds a stronger move and the reply shows why. Check the reply even when the move feels obvious.
Off-pattern, but strong. The human-move model gave this move a low chance, and the engine still rates it strong. Learn what makes it work.
Hard defense missed. One move held among those we checked, and the human-move model reads that defense as hard to spot. Set it up and drill it.
Hard find, and it's the best. The engine ranks this move first, and the human-move model and the alternatives we checked rate it difficult to spot. Bank the idea.
Tough defense, found. This kept the position playable when the other moves we checked didn't, and the human-move model reads it as hard to find. Strong work.
Natural and best. The human-move model sees it coming, and the engine puts it on top. Good instinct; keep the why with it.
Natural pick, strong result. The human-move model expects it, and the engine rates it strong, with another move as its top choice. Check what the top choice adds.
Clock nearly empty. The clock was almost out when this move was played. Factor that in when reviewing the decision.
Fast move. Snap decision, time still in the bank. Make sure the speed matched the position.
Long think. Heavy clock spend on this move. Check whether the position called for it.
Opening identified. The line is on record. That says where the game is, not whether the move is good.
Book's done. The game leaves the opening book's line right here. From now on, every move has to stand on its own reasons.
Recovered. Setback absorbed, and the position holds again. Line up the setback and the recovery side by side.
Recovered, with help. The position is playable again after the earlier setback, and errors by the other side made that possible. Note both parts.
Opportunity taken. The opponent's last move left a chance, and this move cashes it in. That's the response to train.
Opportunity missed. The opponent's last move left a chance, and this one lets it slide. Rewind one move and find what changed.
Repeat pattern. This exact problem is back for another round in this game. Put the moments side by side and find the shared trigger.
Cover restored. The piece that was hanging earlier has a guard again. Pinpoint the new guard.
Slow leak. This is another small concession, and together they've worn the position down. Pull the full sequence, not just this move.
Conversion complete. No slip at all, right through to the recorded win. Replay that stretch and log how it held.
Recurring pattern. Same issue, more saved games. Gather those positions into one drill set.
Checkmate. Attacked king, zero legal squares. Run the final moves back once more to lock in the pattern.
Checkmate, defense over. Zero legal squares left for the king. Find the earlier point where the defense could still have changed.
Draw. The result is set, but the decisions along the way still need reviewing.
Focus up. Read the position, find the key pattern, then make your move.
Miss. That attempt fails. Reset, scan again and pick a different candidate.
Blank result on that attempt. Go again with the move.
Forced mate. The saved engine analysis gives the side that played this move a forced checkmate. That's the headline.
Mate against. Per the saved engine analysis, this move lets the other side force checkmate.
Material up. Through the saved line, the side that made this move ends ahead of where the line started.
Material down. Through the saved line, the side that made this move ends behind where the line started.
Accepted. The exercise takes this move, but the moves shown don't give a clear tactical reason to point at.
Not accepted. The exercise rejects this move, and the moves shown don't give a clear tactical reason either way.
Match. This is one of the exercise's saved answers, and those answers decide what counts here.
No match. This move isn't one of the exercise's saved answers. That's a rule of the exercise, not a verdict on the chess.
Study the move, then go straight to the next position.
Good move. Lock in the reason it works along with the move.
Practice logged. Your review schedule stays put.
Solved. The relearning flag on this recall stays up.
Start position. Nothing has moved yet in the line we're about to run.
Next up. Spot what this move changes.
Check. The reply has to handle the king before anything else.
Out of check. The king is safe from that attack after this move.
Promotion. Last rank reached, and the pawn is now a new piece.
Promotion with check. The pawn becomes a new piece on the last rank, and it attacks the king at once.
Promotion and mate. The new piece lands, and the king is out of legal squares.
Promotion, out of check. Reaching the last rank also lifts the check on its own king.
Capture. A piece leaves the board for good.
Capture with check. One move removes a piece and attacks the king.
Capture and mate. One move removes a piece and leaves the king with no legal escape.
Capture, out of check. Taking that piece ends the check too.
Capture and promotion. The pawn captures its way onto the last rank and turns into a new piece.
Capture, promotion, check. The pawn takes on the last rank, promotes, and the new piece attacks the king.
Capture, promotion, mate. The pawn takes on the last rank, promotes, and the king has no legal way out.
Capture, promotion, out of check. The pawn takes on the last rank, promotes, and its own king is safe from the check.
Castling with check. The rook lands on its new square and attacks the enemy king.
Castling into mate. The rook lands on its new square and the enemy king has no legal escape.
Fork cashed in. One piece hits several targets, then takes one of them, and this example ends with a net material gain for that side.
Pinned, can't capture. That piece is tied to its king, so the marked capture would expose the king and isn't legal.
Pinned, can't run. The attacked piece is tied to its king, so it's limited to moves along the pin line.
Pinned defenders. They're tied to their king and can't take back, which is why the capture works. Material ends up ahead by the close of the line shown.
Pinned piece, collected. It can't leave the line without exposing its king, and as the moves play out, it's taken.
Skewer cashed in. The front piece moves off the line, and the piece behind it is taken along that same line.
King skewer. The king, in check, steps aside, which exposes the piece behind it to the same attacker, and it falls.
Sole defender down. It's captured first, and later in these moves the piece it was guarding goes too.
Deflection cashed in. The defender is pulled off its job, and the piece it was covering is captured.
Discovery cashed in. The blocking piece moves, the line opens, and the piece behind makes the capture.
Discovered check. The front piece moves aside, and the one behind it checks the king.
Double check. Two pieces attack the king at once, so the only answer is a king move.
Double attack cashed in. The moving piece makes one threat and unmasks a second, and that second attacker makes the capture here.
Promotion, and material up. Once the pawn promotes, this example finishes with a net material gain for that side.
Loose piece taken. Nothing protects it, so no recapture follows, and this example ends with that side ahead in material.
Pin released. The opponent's previous move freed the attacking piece from a relative pin, the target stayed put, and the line shown ends with it captured.
Marked reply. The other side is allowed to play it. Put it on the board and run the line.
Scan first for any piece of yours that could be taken with no useful recapture.
No quiet move until the board is swept for loose enemy pieces.
Forcing-move sweep: hunt for a single piece able to hit two valuable targets.
Every pinned piece is covering for something. Confirm whether that's your king or a bigger piece before it moves.
Read past the front target. A line attack can carry through to something valuable behind it.
Before you trade off a defender, list everything it's covering.
When a blocking piece moves, scan the lines it uncovers.
Hunt for one move with two threats, counting checks and freshly opened lines.
Before a back-rank defender leaves, confirm your king still has an exit.
Count every advanced pawn's steps to promotion, and check the pawn pushes that force a reply.
Before a defender moves, list the pieces that would lose their cover.
Score the full trade: your capture, then their recapture.
Check whether a forcing exchange could drag a defender off another job.
Saved answers rule this exercise. Other legal moves can still be playable chess.
Strong replies, one possible line. Treat none of them as forced.
Material is scored only inside the line shown, counted from its first position. Piece values: see the written explanation.
No simple tactical reason shows up in the saved line, and no positional reason has been assumed. Walk it move by move and weigh each reply.
The saved answer policy for this exercise drives this explanation; check the written notes for which one.
Here's the opening line you're drilling. Run the moves in order.
Correct. Matches your study material exactly.
Go with one of your study-line moves.
Every move in your chosen lines is good for this one.
Recall it: play the move your study material has here.
Off your opening lines. Go again.
Off your opening lines. Go again. The study changed, so this saved attempt leaves its review schedule as is.
Off your opening lines. Go again. This position is retired, so its review schedule doesn't move.
Mixed Due takes this line's moves. Dedicated practice drills it solo.
Scheduled recalls ask for your selected side's moves, and a position your active studies share gets one card.
Saved session needs a reload. Do that, then move.
Playing the verified line now. Eyes on every move.
Logged as revealed. Replay the solution below when you're ready.
Solved on the retry. Both the miss and the finish go on record.
Clean solve. Zero wrong moves, first to last. That's execution.
Wrong move for this puzzle. The right ones you already played stay saved.
Correct. Keep the run going.
Work the line out first, then move. Take the time it needs.
Not enough engine data to explain this position. Explore it on the board instead.
Review's paused. Resume below, or test ideas by moving a piece.
Tap a move to review it, or play a piece to test your own idea.
